stories.delivered_paragraph: Elon Musk’s xAI, now owned by SpaceX, sued Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison to block a state law targeting apps that create non-consensual sexualized images. The law, due to take effect Saturday, allows fines of $500,000 each time a user creates an explicit deepfake; xAI argues it is an overbroad, content-based restriction on speech. The case will test how far states can regulate generative-AI tools used for image manipulation.

stories.delivered_paragraph: The Federal Communications Commission announced an import ban on foreign-made “advanced robotic devices” and power inverters, citing unacceptable risks, in a move expected to hit Chinese manufacturers hardest. The restriction covers mobile devices including humanoid and quadruped robots, while China is also home to major inverter suppliers used in solar arrays. The policy extends Washington’s technology-security campaign into emerging robotics and clean-energy hardware supply chains.

stories.delivered_paragraph: Providence Equity Partners will become the majority investor in THE•TEAM, the talent and sports agency formerly known as Wasserman, by providing additional capital for the company to buy founder Casey Wasserman’s remaining stake. Providence has been an investor since 2022, and Mike Watt, president since 2014, will become CEO when the deal closes. Financial terms were not disclosed, ending a sale process launched after Wasserman said in February that he would sell.

stories.delivered_paragraph: The Federal Aviation Administration is moving to waive environmental rules for some launch approvals, a step that could speed work by companies including SpaceX and Blue Origin. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the administration wants to remove government “red tape” to preserve U.S. leadership in the space race. The change could shorten permitting timelines, though it also reduces a layer of environmental review around a rapidly expanding launch industry.

stories.delivered_paragraph: Seattle residents and Mayor Bruce Harrell gathered for a candlelight vigil after a gunfight at the Bite of Seattle food festival killed three people and injured at least four others. The victims were Junior Cee Niko Semo, 19, Carlos Israel Sanchez Villalba, 44, and Ashley Whitehead, 56; the free three-day festival typically draws about 350,000 people. The killings have turned a major civic event into a renewed focus for public-safety concerns.

stories.delivered_paragraph: Senate Majority Leader John Thune and House Speaker Mike Johnson plan to attend President Trump’s two-day midterm convention in Dallas in September, underscoring their effort to maintain party unity. Other Republican candidates, including Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, also intend to attend, while Maine Sen. Susan Collins is unlikely to do so. The gathering offers fundraising and media exposure but puts vulnerable Republicans close to a president whose approval ratings are falling.

stories.delivered_paragraph: President Donald Trump and the Justice Department separately asked the Supreme Court to erase the $83.3 million defamation verdict won by writer E. Jean Carroll. Trump argues he was immune because his 2019 statements denying Carroll’s sexual-assault claim were made while president; the DOJ says the federal government should have replaced him as defendant, which would have ended the claim. The appeals seek to expand protections for presidents and federal employees over official conduct.

Its advancement signals broad Senate interest in tougher economic measures, though the scope and timing of final action remain unsettled.

stories.delivered_paragraph: The Senate voted 86-12 to advance a Russia and Iran sanctions bill championed by the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, shortly after senators met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. The measure would impose 100% secondary tariffs on countries buying Russian oil and gas and targets Russia’s sanctions-evasion “shadow fleet”; it also renews Iran sanctions due to expire this year. The lopsided procedural vote gives leaders a stronger path toward final passage after months of delay.

stories.delivered_paragraph: Iran’s Revolutionary Guard launched several ballistic missiles at U.S. forces in the Middle East late Tuesday, but U.S. Central Command said all were intercepted. U.S. officials said the apparent target was a base in Jordan, and U.S. crude futures rose more than 4% to $82.50 a barrel after the attack. The exchange ended a two-day lull in fighting and raises pressure on Washington and Tehran’s already fragile diplomatic pause.

stories.delivered_paragraph: Iran fired multiple ballistic missiles toward a U.S. military base in Jordan on Tuesday, its first such attack since President Trump paused strikes against Tehran on Friday; Central Command said every missile was intercepted. It threatens the pause intended to give diplomacy a chance.

stories.delivered_paragraph: Netflix narrowly overtook the BBC as the first place UK viewers say they turn when choosing what to watch, according to Ofcom’s Media Nations report. Netflix was named first by 26% of viewers in 2025, versus 25% for the BBC; among people aged 16 to 24, the gap was 36% to 14%. Ofcom cautioned that methodology changes make year-to-year comparisons indicative, but the findings sharpen pressure on the BBC’s funding model.

stories.delivered_paragraph: Ariana Grande sued unidentified hackers in Los Angeles seeking to uncover people she alleges stole and leaked unreleased music, videos and photographs. The suit says 45 unreleased songs were hacked and leaked in 2023 alone, part of hundreds of alleged leaks since her 2011 debut, and claims the material was taken through producers and photographers in her circle. The case seeks to halt distribution and identify alleged sellers operating through social platforms.

stories.delivered_paragraph: Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey” is on track to exceed the roughly $330 million domestic lifetime total of his 2023 hit “Oppenheimer” after only 13 days in theaters. Its second Monday brought in $14.7 million, with Tuesday projected at more than $16 million. The pace underscores the film’s unusually sustained opening-run demand and places it among the year’s defining box-office successes, while “Hadestown” also posted a $2 million-plus Monday.

stories.delivered_paragraph: Big Ten Commissioner Tony Petitti renewed his call for a 24-team College Football Playoff beginning in 2027, saying quicker action would make the transition easier. Petitti made the case on the opening day of the conference’s media days, keeping the Big Ten at the center of a debate over how much further to expand the postseason. The proposal would substantially widen access but would also reshape scheduling, player workloads and the value of the regular season.

stories.delivered_paragraph: Ford raised its outlook after beating second-quarter earnings expectations, citing operational improvements, resilient vehicle prices and a sales mix tilted toward more profitable models. The updated guidance gives investors evidence that the company’s core combustion-vehicle business is cushioning broader pressure on auto demand.

stories.delivered_paragraph: Micron Technology shares are headed toward their worst monthly decline in 11 years as investors grow more concerned that China is building up domestic supplies of memory chips and chipmaking equipment. Analysts say those fears have weighed on the stock despite continuing interest in semiconductors used for AI systems. The drop highlights a risk for U.S. chipmakers: Chinese self-sufficiency efforts could pressure demand and market share in one of their most important markets.

stories.delivered_paragraph: FIFA is considering a plan to raise billions of dollars by selling minority stakes in commercial rights tied to the World Cup, including to an investment firm run by Joshua Kushner, Jared Kushner’s brother. The proposal would bring outside investors into a share of the tournament’s revenue-generating business rather than the competition itself. It could give FIFA more capital, while also increasing private investors’ influence over the economics of the world’s biggest soccer event.
